title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
summary: Follow specific, two-way connections among Samaritan traditions, Qumran manuscripts and competing Christian authority, with the evidence and limits of every bridge visible.

connections.label: Samaritan texts and sacred authority
connections.heading: The Dead Sea Scrolls question
connections.context: The concrete bridge is 4QpaleoExodᵐ (4Q22): harmonizing readings connect it to the Samaritan Pentateuch, but do not identify its readers. Dayfani’s 2022 reconstruction also challenges the older assumption that the Gerizim composition was absent. Follow [[qumran-text-history|Qumran Text History]] and [[jesus-and-dead-sea-scrolls|Jesus and Dead Sea Scrolls]] with the distinction between preserved wording, reconstruction and institutional allegiance intact.

connections.label: Jesus and Dead Sea Scrolls
connections.context: Compare the authority questions in [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|Samaritan texts and sacred authority]]: shared scripture, priesthood and sacred place can come apart. John 4 directly engages the Samaritan mountain/Jerusalem dispute; shared language with Qumran is a different kind of evidence. These connections do not establish that Jesus’s movement belonged to Qumran or descended from Samaritan institutions.

connections.label: Samaritan and Jewish Texts
connections.context: Read this preserved conversation beside [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|the developed Samaritan inquiry]] and [[qumran-text-history|Qumran Text History]]. The new bridge separates the Samaritan community’s own account of Israelite continuity from textual comparison and modern historical reconstruction. It does not define a living tradition solely through its opponents.

connections.label: Qumran Text History
connections.context: 4QpaleoExodᵐ supplies a specific connection to [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|the Samaritan Pentateuch inquiry]]. The label pre-Samaritan concerns textual affinities, not proof of Samaritan ownership or one universally authoritative library. Compare each passage before moving from a reading to a community.

connections.label: Sacred inheritance and rival continuations
connections.heading: Legitimacy consists of several things that can come apart
connections.context: The [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|Samaritan inquiry]], [[jesus-and-dead-sea-scrolls|Jesus and Dead Sea Scrolls]] and [[tor-thomas-and-gnostic-transmission|Christian transmission inquiry]] now share an explicit reading matrix. It separates shared readings, rival sacred places, direct literary engagement and reported succession, so a connection does not silently become a genealogy.

connections.label: The Teacher, Thomas and Gnostic transmission
connections.context: Clement, Stromata VII.17, reports rival claims linking Basilides to Glaucias/Peter and Valentinus to Theudas/Paul. These are specific ancient pedigree claims, not a demonstrated Samaritan-to-Qumran-to-Christian chain. Compare [[sacred-inheritance-and-rival-continuations|rival inheritances]] and [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|Samaritan authority]] at the level of the claim actually attested.

connections.label: The Living Jesus in Thomas, John and the Synoptics
connections.context: John 4:19–24 directly engages the Samaritan mountain/Jerusalem worship dispute. That gives [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|the Samaritan inquiry]] a firmer connection to a particular Christian text than a general claim about shared light/darkness language. It still does not establish Qumran membership or an institutional descent line.

connections.label: Manuscripts, movements and survival
connections.context: Use [[qumran-text-history|Qumran Text History]] and [[samaritan-texts-and-sacred-authority|Samaritan sacred authority]] to test the steps between a surviving manuscript, textual affinity, religious ownership and social authority. Those are four different claims. A common harmonizing practice cannot supply all four at once.

matrix.question: Which Torah wording?
matrix.limit: A textual relationship does not identify an owner or prove regional authority.

matrix.question: Who defines legitimate worship?
matrix.basis: Gerizim and disputes about ritual or calendar in the scrolls
matrix.limit: Different sacred places and different Temple policies are not one movement.

matrix.question: Does a Christian text discuss Samaritans?
matrix.basis: John 4:19–24: the mountain, Jerusalem, spirit and truth
matrix.limit: Literary engagement does not establish Qumran or Samaritan institutional ancestry.

matrix.question: Whose continuity claim?
matrix.basis: Samaritan Israelite identity and competing accounts of inheritance
matrix.limit: Present the community’s own account without treating it as independent proof.

matrix.question: Whose apostolic pedigree?
matrix.basis: Clement, Stromata VII.17, and competing Christian authority claims
matrix.limit: A reported pedigree is evidence of a claim, not automatic verification.

matrix.question: How much can a manuscript establish?
matrix.basis: Witness, reading, reconstruction, ownership and reception
matrix.limit: Copy date, composition date, narrated event and social influence remain distinct.

staticConnections.label: Dead Sea Scrolls, Jewish diversity and empire
staticConnections.reason: Textual plurality, canon and community authority are different questions.

staticConnections.label: The laughing Jesus in the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter
staticConnections.reason: A particular Christian revelation disputes ecclesiastical authority without supplying a Samaritan ancestry.

staticConnections.label: Dead Sea Scrolls dating and the Teacher: evidence review
staticConnections.reason: Manuscript dating and proposed historical identity are separate from textual affiliation.
